 Your Daily Dose: Daylight saving time, to save or not to save?
 Maybe it’s time we stop messing with the clocks.
 Graphic by Grace Cho
 By
 Grace B. Lee 
 Published Thursday, November 12, 2026 
 Whether you were able to recharge a little more before the Cambridge Half Marathon, extend your Halloweekend a little longer, or just get some additional sleep during a busy midterm season, the end of daylight saving time brings a much-appreciated extra hour of nighttime. Nevertheless, at least personally, watching the sun set during my 3-4:15 p.m. class this week was pretty tough. As frustrating as it might be to lose daylight so early in the evening, the twice-yearly clock change has additional implications that go well beyond our ability to enjoy an evening outside. 
 First introduced in the United States in 1918 , though not standardized as a cyclical biannual shift until 1966 , daylight saving time was created as a wartime measure to save energy and fuel . Contemporary rationale for daylight saving time extends beyond energy savings, with proponents praising the increased economic and physical activity that comes with extended daylight later into the night . 
 Yet, changing the clocks twice a year also comes with a number of challenges, especially regarding our health.   Daylight saving time isn’t just about losing or gaining one hour of sleep; the systematic adjustment of clocks disrupts our circadian rhythm, leading to sleep problems that last beyond the immediate days after the shift.   The biannual shift also leads to increased cardiac events , motor vehicle accidents   and abnormal psychiatric symptoms . 
 Thus, there have been several efforts to eliminate the need to change twice a year.  Currently stalled in the Senate after passing the House of Representatives in July 2025, the Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 was proposed by Representative Vern Buchanan, a Republican from Florida,   as the most recent attempt to make daylight saving time permanent, which would mean later sunrises and later sunsets.   Advocates for the bill often argue that longer evenings will lead to greater physical activity and spending . 
 Making daylight saving time permanent, however, also comes with its challenges. In 2024, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine put out a statement supporting permanent standard time, calling it “the optimal choice for health and safety.”   The professional society defends its position by contending that making daylight saving time permanent creates a persistent mismatch between internal and social clocks, since our circadian rhythms generally depend on the timing of light exposure.   This misalignment can lead to “social jet lag,” which is linked to metabolic, cardiovascular and mental health issues.   Additionally, delayed morning light could lead to a number of safety issues for children, especially an increase in fatalities correlated with dark morning commutes . 
 Endorsed by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine , Representative Mary Gay Scanlon, Democrat of Pennsylvania, introduced the Sunshine for Our Kids Act of 2026 in July, proposing to make standard time, with early sunrises and sunsets, permanent . 
 While it may mean getting used to earlier sunsets and walking to your 6 p.m. class in the dark, permanent standard time could better align our social schedules with our natural sleep schedules, perhaps offering a healthier way forward.  As lawmakers continue to debate the future of daylight saving time, these potential health implications must remain central to the conversation, even when the policy at hand seems as simple as adjusting our alarm clocks.
